quarterly_data.signal: December-quarter 2025 results (KLA fiscal Q2 2026; CEO Richard Wallace, CFO Bren Higgins): revenue $3.3 billion, above the $3.225 billion guidance midpoint, with 17% year-over-year growth 'fueled by investment in leading-edge foundry logic, high bandwidth memory, and DRAM'. Non-GAAP diluted EPS $8.85 and GAAP diluted EPS $8.68, both above the guidance midpoints. Gross margin 62.6%, sixty basis points above the guidance midpoint on stronger-than-modeled service and manufacturing efficiencies; operating margin 42.8%; record quarterly free cash flow of $1.26 billion; services revenue $786 million (up 6% sequentially and 18% year over year), the sixteenth consecutive year of annual service growth. Calendar 2025: revenue grew 17% to a record $12.745 billion, with process control systems revenue up 19% ('outpacing the industry growth by several points') and service up 15%; gross and operating margins of 62% and 43.6%; free cash flow up 30% to $4.4 billion; $3 billion returned to shareholders. Management reiterated a 12% to 14% go-forward target model for service revenue and said drivers suggest operating at the higher end of that range over time.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $3.3 billion (17% year-over-year); CY2025 revenue a record $12.745 billion; gross margin 62.6%; record free cash flow $1.26 billion

quarterly_data.signal: March-quarter guidance and calendar-2026 revenue view (CFO Bren Higgins): March-quarter revenue $3.35 billion, plus or minus $150 million; foundry logic ~60% of revenue from semiconductor customers (consistent with the December quarter) and memory ~40% of semi process-control systems revenue to semiconductor customers. Gross margin guided to 61.75% plus or minus one percentage point (product mix modestly weaker plus rising DRAM cost), and March is 'probably the low point for the year'; calendar-2026 gross margin approximately 62%, plus or minus 50 basis points, with the long-run model still 63% plus. Operating expenses ~$645 million in March, rising by roughly $15 million sequentially through the year; 2026 planning tax rate 14.5%. Calendar 2026 revenue 'will grow mid-single digits compared to 2025, with accelerating growth in the second half of the calendar year' — the first half is supply-limited, and Higgins described second-half growth, half on half, as 'that sort of high single low double range' (he declined to guide the full year more precisely). Management pointed to 'strong customer momentum that has accelerated over the past three months, as reflected in our system backlog and sales funnel', and to the March 12 Investor Day for the 2030 model. (January 2026 point-in-time view.)
quarterly_data.figure: March-quarter revenue $3.35 billion, plus or minus $150 million; CY2026 revenue to grow mid-single digits; CY2026 gross margin approximately 62%, plus or minus 50 basis points

quarterly_data.signal: January 2026 WFE outlook (CFO Bren Higgins) — a point-in-time view: core WFE to grow high single to low double digits, 'reaching the low $120 billion range, up from approximately $110 billion in 2025'; the advanced-packaging component to grow at a similar rate to approximately $12 billion, 'for a total market forecast in the mid-$130 billion range' (Higgins said this is consistent with what Lam said the day before). By segment, KLA models foundry logic WFE up 10% to 15% and the DRAM part of the market up 15% to 20% in 2026 ('driven mostly by the demands for HBM'), with flash slower than DRAM off a lower base; advanced logic and DRAM are the biggest WFE growth drivers. For KLA, the foundry-logic business is expected to be stronger in the second half than the first. Wallace: some customers are 'definitely facility constrained', and in foundry logic the 'setup for 27 is pretty remarkable', with discussions already under way with equipment suppliers about 2027. He also said foundry customers are broadening and process-control intensity is going up this year, driven by technology node, die size and design mix.
quarterly_data.figure: core WFE low $120 billion range (from approximately $110 billion in 2025); total mid-$130 billion range; foundry logic 10% to 15%, DRAM 15% to 20%

quarterly_data.signal: Supply-constrained first half (CFO Bren Higgins, CEO Richard Wallace): 'as it relates to the first half, we're virtually sold out across most of our products', because first-half shipments reflect decisions made in 2025 given KLA's lead times. Customer lead times are extending on supply constraints, which limits first-half growth across many products. The biggest long-lead-time part of KLA's bill of materials is optical components — Wallace: optics capacity 'you can add it, but you can't add it quickly' — so the constraint is product-specific, not customer-specific. KLA has been trying to add capacity in the BBP product line and Wallace said 'probably we're going to need it based on our conversations with customers'. Demand is for leading-edge solutions; new-order conversations are mostly 'for deliveries late in '26 and into '27', and customers are also limited by facility readiness (their ability to build new fabs and shells). Higgins said KLA is not losing business and balances allocation across customers. Wallace added that in some cases customers are back-penetrating newer capability onto prior technology nodes to squeeze out more yield.
quarterly_data.figure: virtually sold out across most of our products (first half 2026); new orders for deliveries late in '26 and into '27

quarterly_data.signal: China (CFO Bren Higgins, CEO Richard Wallace): China WFE is expected to be 'flattish, maybe slightly positive' in 2026 after being modestly negative in 2025; total China WFE including restricted fabs is seen in the 'mid to high $30 billion range in 2026'. China is expected to be in the 'mid 20% to high 20% range' of KLA's revenue. Three months earlier KLA expected its China business to be modestly down; it now expects it to be up this year, as business affected by the affiliate rule 'has come back in and feathered through within our forecast'. On competition, Wallace said Chinese domestic suppliers have made more progress in process tools than in lithography or process control, and KLA's main China challenge is when it is not permitted to sell while non-US companies are; KLA wants a level playing field.
quarterly_data.figure: China WFE mid to high $30 billion range in 2026; China mid 20% to high 20% range of KLA revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Where process-control share is growing (CFO Bren Higgins, CEO Richard Wallace): reticle inspection 'had a really strong year' and should stay very strong because it is 'so tied to the number of design starts'; KLA sees 'some positive momentum in our electron beam businesses'; its largest businesses (broadband plasma and high-end pattern inspection) serve a market growing faster than others, where KLA has strong share; metrology is 'historically a little closer tied to some of the capacity' and should see some relative recovery. Wallace said KLA feels 'really good about the trends' it is seeing, especially in inspection and the BBP products. Management expects to sustain multi-year outperformance versus WFE despite a heavier memory mix, because HBM is 'changing the intensity profile'. Per Wallace, AI build-out drivers are more designs and larger die.

HBM and DRAM process-control intensity, January 2026 view (CEO Richard Wallace, CFO Bren Higgins): Wallace said HBM 'has become a huge driver' and 'In many ways, a bigger story is the change intensity around memory', with heavy use of advanced inspection. DRAM intensity is rising because (1) device value is higher, so customers give less real estate to redundancy, (2) moving more data requires more metallization layers that need inspection, and (3) more advanced (EUV) lithography requires more inspection — so DRAM 'looks much more similar to what logic did not that long ago'. Higgins added that with high-performance compute, customers can no longer bin devices, which drives more rigor to ensure 'each of the devices in the stacks' performs to tight specs; it also opens more service-contract penetration as customers keep tools at maximum uptime. Asked whether DRAM intensity could approach advanced logic, Wallace said it is 'still a ways away from advanced logic given the high mix of designs' and he was not ready to commit to that. KLA models the DRAM part of WFE up 15% to 20% in 2026, 'driven mostly by the demands for HBM'. March-quarter mix: memory approximately 40% of semi process-control systems revenue to semiconductor customers, with DRAM roughly 85% and NAND the remaining 15%.
quarterly_data.figure: memory approximately 40% of semi process-control systems revenue (March quarter), DRAM roughly 85%; DRAM WFE 15% to 20% growth in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: DRAM price spike hits KLA's own cost (CFO Bren Higgins): March-quarter gross-margin guidance includes 'the incremental impact of the rapidly escalating cost of DRAM' used in the image-processing computers that ship with KLA systems. The pricing environment 'has changed profoundly over the past two to three months'; KLA expects it to be transitory, but current modeling says it will persist through 2026 with a 'roughly 75 to 100 basis points negative impact on gross margins for the calendar year'. 'As DRAM capacity additions accelerate over the next several quarters, we expect this cost dynamic to improve as we exit the calendar year', with a return to normalized memory pricing modeled in longer-term forecasts. KLA's 'first priority as it relates to memory supply is securing supply to ensure that we can meet our delivery commitments'; its pricing is value-based rather than tied to commodity cost moves. Separately, tariffs carry 'a 50 to a 100 basis point impact', currently near the top end and expected to come down through 2026. (January 2026 point-in-time view.)
quarterly_data.figure: roughly 75 to 100 basis points negative impact on gross margins for the calendar year (2026)

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging, January 2026 view (CEO Richard Wallace, CFO Bren Higgins): KLA's advanced-packaging 'calendar 2025 total systems revenue of $950 million representing over 70% year-over-year growth', and for calendar 2026 it expected 'year-over-year percentage growth expectations in the mid to high teens driven by faster than market growth for our process control products'. Higgins sized the advanced-packaging equipment market at roughly $11 billion in 2025, growing to 'somewhere in excess of $12 billion' in 2026, and said it is a quicker-turn business. Asked why growth looked lower than the >20% view from the October call, Higgins said the market is small so percentages move around, putting growth 'in that we'll call it 10% to 20% range'. Share: Higgins said that in 2021, in process control, 'we were roughly 10% of that market', versus 'close to half the market' in 2025, with high sampling rates and a broader portfolio customers will leverage more. Management said customers are frustrated by the facility space available for packaging, which slows 2026 growth, so 'we'll see a lot more growth in '27'. (January 2026 point-in-time view.)
quarterly_data.figure: calendar 2025 total systems revenue of $950 million (over 70% year-over-year growth); 2026 growth mid to high teens; process-control share roughly 10% (2021) to close to half the market (2025)

quarterly_data.signal: NAND is the small part of KLA's memory business (CFO Bren Higgins, CEO Richard Wallace): in March-quarter guidance, memory is approximately 40% of semi process-control systems revenue, with DRAM roughly 85% and NAND the remaining 15%. For 2026 WFE, Higgins said flash is 'a little harder to pin', growing slower than DRAM off a lower base. Asked whether NAND makers' more aggressive spending talk could change the view, Wallace said that with industry supply constraints, any new demand showing up today is 'more about 27 deliveries'.
